title: AI is positioned to expand trade and productivity, but digital capability gaps and fragmented rules may concentrate the gains
source_unit: WTO, World Trade Report 2025: Making trade and AI work together to the benefit of all
geography: Global trade and AI scenarios across economies, sectors, firms, workers, and digital-trade policy environments

observations.period: 2025-2040; modeled AI and trade expansion scenarios

denominator.unit: WTO global trade-and-AI model scenario frame

global_trade_increase.unit: percent projected increase in global trade by 2040 across AI uptake and catch-up scenarios

global_gdp_increase.unit: percent projected global GDP increase across modeled AI scenarios

digitally_deliverable_services_trade.unit: percent projected increase in digitally deliverable services trade across the report's scenarios

observations.method: WTO Global Trade Model scenarios incorporating AI services, reductions in trade costs, task shifts from labour to AI, productivity gains, and differing degrees of policy and technological catch-up.
observations.uncertainty: These are model scenarios, not forecasts; results depend on AI productivity, adoption, trade costs, labour substitution/complementarity, digital infrastructure, skills, policy, and regulatory conditions.
observations.subgroup: Economies, sectors, workers, firms, digitally deliverable services, and economies at different levels of digital infrastructure and AI capability.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trade and GDP gains can coexist with job displacement, skill premia, regional concentration, unequal bargaining power, and environmental or social costs; aggregate growth is not inclusive by definition.

observations.period: 2025-2040; digital catch-up, infrastructure, skills, and distribution

denominator.unit: WTO scenario comparison for low-, middle-, and high-income economies

low_income_income_gain.unit: percent projected income increase for low-income economies in a scenario narrowing the digital-infrastructure gap by half and increasing AI adoption

middle_income_income_gain.unit: percent projected income increase for middle-income economies under the comparable catch-up scenario

inclusion_conditions.value: digital infrastructure, skills, capabilities, education, training, labour-market policy, and open trade
inclusion_conditions.unit: policy conditions identified as shaping inclusive AI-enabled trade

observations.method: WTO comparison of AI uptake scenarios with different degrees of digital infrastructure catch-up, capability diffusion, and policy support across income groups.
observations.uncertainty: Scenario gains are conditional and do not measure realized income, job quality, firm survival, or household access; closing an infrastructure gap does not guarantee equitable ownership or bargaining power.
observations.subgroup: Low- and middle-income economies, small firms, workers requiring reskilling, digital-service providers, education and training systems, and communities outside high-capability clusters.
observations.counterinterpretation: Catch-up can expand participation but may also increase dependence on foreign platforms, infrastructure, data, capital, or standards; digital access is not the same as local control.

observations.period: 2012-2025; AI-enabling goods, trade restrictions, and regulatory fragmentation

denominator.unit: global AI-related goods and digital-trade policy frame

ai_goods_trade_2023.unit: US dollars in global trade of AI-enabling goods in 2023, approximately

quantitative_restrictions_2012.unit: quantitative restrictions applied to AI-related goods in 2012

quantitative_restrictions_2024.unit: nearly number of quantitative restrictions applied to AI-related goods in 2024

low_income_bound_tariff.unit: percent; upper bound of tariffs on some AI-enabling goods in some low-income economies

observations.method: WTO analysis of AI-enabling goods trade, tariff and quantitative-restriction data, digital-trade regulation, and risks of policy fragmentation.
observations.uncertainty: Restriction counts do not measure restrictiveness, enforcement, welfare effects, or whether policies are justified by security, safety, or industrial goals; tariff incidence varies by product, firm, and supply chain.
observations.subgroup: AI hardware and intermediate-input producers, small and large firms, importing economies, consumers, workers, regulators, and economies dependent on foreign digital infrastructure or technology.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some restrictions can address security, safety, competition, or resilience concerns; open trade alone does not guarantee trustworthy AI, labour protection, or inclusive distribution.

related_sources.claim: WTO AI for Trade programme and applied case-study context.
WTO trade outlook context for AI-related goods and 2026 trade risks.

boundary: This record adds an AI-to-trade, capability-diffusion, labour, small-firm, regulatory-fragmentation, and geopolitical-dependence route. It is not firm respondent microdata, an individual employment forecast, a causal estimate of AI adoption, or proof that modeled aggregate gains will be broadly shared.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official WTO report page, full report PDF, AI for Trade page, launch news item, and trade-outlook context were retrieved; model ranges, digital catch-up conditions, AI-enabling goods trade, restrictions, and tariff claims were cross-checked.
